hops.title: One receptor gene changes how a floral note smells
hops.text: Two people can sniff the same drink and describe it quite differently. Food makers add beta-ionone for a pleasant floral note, yet people differ enormously in how well they detect it. In 2013, researchers traced it to a single amino-acid change in one odorant receptor, OR5A1. The authors report that it explains over 96 percent of the observed variation, so sensitivity behaves almost like a single-gene trait. Sensitive people more easily tell which samples have added beta-ionone and often call it fragrant or floral, and the genotype also predicted different food and product choices. One receptor line reads the molecule differently, and what the person smells changes with it.

sources.citation: Jaeger SR et al., Curr Biol 23(16):1601-1605 (2013)

image.caption: A one-amino-acid change in receptor OR5A1 shifts how strongly beta-ionone's floral note comes through.

hops.afterHeading: Sour and salt: the channel routes
hops.title: The champagne blues and the sour cells that taste fizz
hops.text: In 1988, two authors gave a strange drug side effect a memorable name: the champagne blues. Patients taking acetazolamide, which blocks the enzyme carbonic anhydrase, reported that carbonated drinks tasted abnormal. That hinted carbonic anhydrase had a job in taste. Twenty-one years later, Charles Zuker's team silenced specific taste-cell classes in mice and found which cells use it. The sour-sensing cells are the taste sensors for carbonation, using carbonic anhydrase 4 to detect carbon dioxide. In mice lacking that enzyme, the taste nerve responded far less to carbon dioxide. A soda's tingle also comes from touch and irritation nerves, but its taste, in mice at least, runs through sour cells.

sources.citation: Graber M & Kelleher S, Am J Med 84(5):979-980 (1988); Kehrenberg MCA & Bachmann HS, Naunyn Schmiedebergs Arch Pharmacol 395(6):619-627 (2022)

image.caption: In mice, carbonic anhydrase 4 lets sour taste cells signal the carbon dioxide in fizzy drinks.

hops.afterHeading: Back to the puzzles, and where the rule stops
hops.title: Why a head cold makes food bland
hops.text: If you have had a bad head cold, you have probably noticed food go bland. Much of that loss is smell rather than taste: aromas from food in your mouth reach the nose from behind, by retronasal smell, and a cold weakens that route. When researchers in Dresden tested 58 people during an acute cold, their retronasal smell was reduced, and so was their sensitivity to salt. People blame their tongues anyway. In a University of Pennsylvania study of 750 smell-and-taste clinic patients, complaints of taste loss usually reflected a loss of smell, with upper respiratory infections among the top causes of lasting smell loss.

sources.citation: Deems DA et al., Arch Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 117(5):519-528 (1991)
Pellegrino R et al., Int Forum Allergy Rhinol 7(2):185-191 (2017)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A student in a scarf on a couch beside a tissue box, holding a steaming bowl of soup and looking puzzled.
image.caption: A cold weakens retronasal smell, which is why food seems bland while the tongue gets the blame.
